line.ohmail: Mail from people you said yes to.
line.ohcal: The calendars you already have, in one place.

server.label: Your server’s address
server.hint: It is the address you open ohmail at in a browser, with nothing after the host.

certificate.android: A private name needs a certificate from an authority Android already trusts, and a root you install yourself does not count. A public name or a Tailscale address always works.
certificate.ios: A private name works once you install its root and switch it on under Certificate Trust Settings. A public name or a Tailscale address always works.

computer.say: Scan the code on my computer.

line.android: ohmail on that computer does the organizing, and this phone keeps a copy.
line.ios: On an iPhone, use the Tailscale address that pane also shows.

computer.iosNote: ohmail cannot yet verify a computer reached over your own network here.

while.android: It organizes while its notification is shown. Dismiss the notification to stop.
while.ios: It organizes while ohmail is open. When you leave the app, it hands the mailbox back.

terms.serverKeeps: Your mail server keeps everything. Nothing here is a copy you could lose.
terms.screener: Mail from the last 60 days from senders you have not decided about moves to the Screener. Older mail, and mail you have filed, stays where it is.

form.nameHint: Shown to the people you write to, beside your address.
form.appOnlyNote: Some work, school and Advanced Protection accounts cannot create App Passwords, and ohmail cannot connect those yet.

hand.say: My server is at <address></address>, and its pairing token is <token></token>.
hand.line: The whole pairing link fits into the token’s blank too.
hand.note: For a computer on your own network, scan its code instead. The address alone is not enough.

confirm.line: A code cannot be read by eye, so check what answered before it is spent.

what.computer: The ohmail app on a computer
what.local: The ohmail app on a computer on your network

confirm.keyFine: The same characters stand under Settings › Devices on that computer. If they differ, something else is answering for it, so do not pair.
confirm.noKeyFine: This address carries a certificate your phone checks on its own, so there is no key to compare by eye.

paired.line: Opening the copy of your mail on this phone.

upgrade.migrating: Updating the mail store on this phone…
upgrade.migratingOf: Updating the mail store on this phone… ({applied} of {pending})
upgrade.migratingSlow: This can take several minutes on a large mailbox.

servers.title: Servers
servers.openingLine: Opening the copy on this phone
servers.syncFailed: Sync failed, and the copy on this phone keeps what it has.
servers.certificateRefused: This phone would not accept the certificate at that address, so it did not send anything. The server needs an https certificate from an authority this phone already trusts.
servers.pairEnded: The pairing ended, so pair this phone again.
servers.ownLine: The mailbox this phone opened itself.
servers.forgetNote: Forgetting deletes the pairing and the mail this phone had copied.
servers.removeNote: Removing it hands the mailbox back, stops ohmail from filing it here, and deletes the mail this phone had copied.

cloud.name: ohmail Cloud
cloud.line: Scan the code under Settings › Devices on the web.

server.name: Your own server
server.line: Give its address, then scan its code.

line.android: Scan the code under Settings › Devices there.
line.ios: Scan its code, or on an iPhone use its Tailscale address.

line.android: Only while the app is open, or behind its notification.
line.ios: Only while the app is open.

remove.title: Stop and remove.
remove.drafts: {count, plural, one {Removing it deletes the unsent draft on this phone. No mail server has it.} other {Removing it deletes the # unsent drafts on this phone. No mail server has them.}}
remove.draftsUnknown: Removing it deletes any unsent drafts on this phone. No mail server has them.
remove.settingsAnswer: Settings you changed on this phone are not in the mailbox yet. They wait for your answer to the settings question above your mail. Answer it first, or removing deletes them.
remove.settingsNewer: Settings you changed on this phone are not in the mailbox, because a newer ohmail saved the mailbox’s settings. Update ohmail first, or removing deletes them.
remove.settingsUnsaved: Settings you changed on this phone could not be saved to the mailbox, so nothing was removed. Removing it now deletes them.
remove.settingsUnknown: Removing it may delete settings you changed on this phone that are not in the mailbox yet.

note.stopPending: A stop is already pending, and it waits for the mailbox.
note.sibling: Another copy of this phone still holds the mailbox’s claim. The stop finishes when that claim lapses.
note.handedBack: Another computer can take this mailbox now.
note.paused: Organizing paused while the account was closed, and it resumes on its own.
note.none: Nothing organizes this mailbox now. Organize it from this phone while ohmail is running on it?
note.readerUnnamed: Another install organizes this mailbox. This phone reads it, and it moves nothing and screens nothing.
note.server: The server you paired with organizes this mailbox, whether or not ohmail is open on this phone. This phone reads it, and it moves nothing and screens nothing.
note.ios: It organizes while ohmail is open. When you leave the app, it hands the mailbox back.
note.battery: Battery saver does not let ohmail organize in the background on this phone. It organizes while the app is open, and hands the mailbox back when you leave.
note.notificationsOff: Notifications are off, so organizing runs only while the app is open.
note.late: When ohmail last left the screen, it could not hand the mailbox back in time, so another machine could not take it for up to {minutes, plural, one {# minute} other {# minutes}}.
note.unsynced: This mailbox’s settings cannot be saved to or read from the mail server, and ohmail keeps trying.
note.startFailed: This phone could not start organizing that mailbox and nothing changed, so try again in a moment.
note.unreadable: This phone could not read whether another computer organizes this mailbox. Nothing changed, so try again.
note.stopFailed: This phone could not hand that mailbox back and is still organizing it, so try again in a moment.

stopAsk.title: Stop organizing here.
stopAsk.what: This phone stops filing this mailbox and goes on reading it. Your folders and everything in them stay where they are.
stopAsk.after: Any install can take it over afterwards, including this one.

background.title: Organizing in the background.
background.why: ohmail shows a notification while it organizes your mailbox in the background. Without it, organizing stops when you leave the app.

newMail.title: New mail

say.on: While ohmail is running, your server tells this phone that something changed, and the app fetches your mail directly. If you close the app, a plain “New mail” notice arrives instead, and tapping it opens ohmail. Either way the signal carries no subject, no sender and no count.
say.noDistributor: No push distributor is chosen on this phone, so nothing wakes this app between visits. A distributor is a separate app you choose yourself, and no Google or Apple push service is involved either way. Mail arrives when you open the app or pull to refresh.
say.ios: Nothing wakes this app between visits on this phone. Mail arrives when you open the app or pull to refresh.
say.desktopHost: Wake notifications need a hosted server. Paired with a desktop, this app syncs when you open it and when you pull to refresh.
say.noKey: This server has not set up a signing key, so it cannot send wake notifications this phone would accept. Whoever runs it can generate one. Mail still arrives when you open the app or pull to refresh.
say.refused: Your distributor’s address was refused by the server, so wake notifications are off. Mail still arrives when you open the app or pull to refresh.
say.failed: Wake notifications could not be set up. Mail still arrives when you open the app or pull to refresh.
say.switchedOff: Notifications for new mail are switched off on this phone, so nothing wakes ohmail while it is closed. Mail still arrives when you open the app or pull to refresh.
say.rowRemains: Wake notifications are off on this phone. Your server would not remove the registration, so it may keep trying the old address for a while. Try again, or revoke this device from the server’s Devices list.

newMail.noneNote: Turning this off stops wake notifications and removes the registration from your server.
newMail.distributorNote: The app that carries the wake signal to this phone. You choose it, you can change it, and it is the only thing in the path besides your own server.

yourName.title: Your name
yourName.label: Name
yourName.failed: That did not save, so try again.
yourName.note: It stands beside your address on the mail you send from this phone. Leave it empty to send with the address alone.

onThisPhone.title: On this phone
onThisPhone.forgetting: Forgetting a server deletes its pairing and the mail this phone had copied. Deleting the app takes the copied mail with it, and the pairing is never included in a backup.
onThisPhone.keychainIos: On an iPhone the pairing stays in the keychain until ohmail is opened again, which discards it before opening anything. To end it straight away, revoke this device from the server’s Devices list.

backup.out: The copied mail is not in a backup either. This app’s stored mail is marked to stay out of the phone’s cloud and computer backups, and this build read that mark back.
backup.in: The copied mail is in a backup. It lives in this app’s stored files, which the phone’s cloud and computer backups include.
backup.unknown: Whether the copied mail is included in a backup could not be read on this build, so nothing here claims it either way.

onThisPhone.deleteNote: Deleting an account needs your second factor, so it happens on your account page in a browser.

diagnostics.title: Diagnostic file
diagnostics.about: One file about how ohmail is running on this phone: versions, counts, error codes and recent log events, never addresses, subjects or folder names. Nothing is sent.
diagnostics.written: Written to {file}, beside this phone’s copied mail, and nothing was sent. Share it with us yourself if you want us to look.
diagnostics.failed: The file could not be written, so nothing was sent.
diagnostics.shareFailed: This phone could not open the share sheet. The file is still where it was written, and nothing was sent.

phoneRefusal.accountErased: This ohmail account was deleted, so its copy of your mail is gone from this phone. The mail on your mail server is untouched.
phoneRefusal.admitCannotPin: Pairing with a computer on your own network is not available in this build of the ohmail app yet. Use the Tailscale address from that computer’s Settings › Devices instead. It works on every platform.
phoneRefusal.admitCleartext: That address is a plain, unencrypted connection, and ohmail will not send your mail over one. A desktop running ohmail serves a secure address, so open Settings › Devices there and use the code it shows.
phoneRefusal.admitNoPin: That pairing code does not carry this computer’s identity, so ohmail cannot tell its connection apart from anything else on your network. Make a fresh code under Settings › Devices in the desktop app and scan that.
phoneRefusal.admitPinNotStored: ohmail could not record this computer’s identity on this phone, so it stopped rather than connecting without it.
phoneRefusal.admitPinUnenforceable: This pairing code carries a key, but its address is a named one whose certificate this phone checks for itself. The key cannot be checked, and ohmail will not show it as if it had been. Use the code shown on the computer or server you mean to pair with.
phoneRefusal.baseApiMixed: One of the two addresses ohmail tried answered and was not its mail API, and the other could not be reached — {0}. If you run this server, check that it is passing /api through to the ohmail API.
phoneRefusal.baseApiNotFound: That address answers, but ohmail could not find its mail API, neither at the address itself nor under /api. If you run this server, check that its proxy passes /api through to the ohmail API.
phoneRefusal.baseApiStopped: That server started answering and then stopped, so ohmail stopped waiting. If you run it, check that its proxy passes requests through to the ohmail API.
phoneRefusal.baseApiTimeout: That server did not answer in time, so ohmail stopped waiting. It may be the network between this phone and it, or a route on the server that never replies.
phoneRefusal.baseApiUnreachable: ohmail could not reach that server to find its mail API — {0}
phoneRefusal.baseCleartext: That is a plain, unencrypted address, and ohmail will not send your mail over one. Give the https address you open ohmail at in a browser.
phoneRefusal.baseNeedsTheCode: That is a numeric address on a network, and no certificate authority can vouch for one. ohmail can only trust it through the code your computer shows, so open Settings › Devices there and scan that instead.
phoneRefusal.baseNotAnAddress: That does not look like a server address. Give the address you open ohmail at in a browser, for example ohmail.example.com, with nothing after the host.
phoneRefusal.bootAccountMismatch: This sign-in belongs to another account than the one named, so ohmail opened nothing. Check which account it should open.

phoneRefusal.pinChanged: This computer’s identity has changed since you paired with it, so ohmail stopped rather than trusting it. If you reinstalled ohmail on that computer or restored it from a backup, open Settings › Devices there and pair this phone again with a fresh code. If you did not, something on your network is answering for it.
